bank.q: King John seals the Magna Carta at Runnymede.
bank.w: Runnymede, June 1215 — the king first put his seal under the law. He ignored it within weeks.

bank.q: The Black Death reaches Europe aboard Genoese merchant ships.
bank.w: Autumn 1347, at Messina — within five years perhaps a third of the continent was gone.

bank.q: Gutenberg prints his 42-line Bible, the first major book made with movable type.
bank.w: Mainz, around 1455 — about 180 copies, and Europe was never private again.

bank.q: Columbus makes landfall in the Americas.
bank.w: October 12, 1492 — an island in the Bahamas he insisted on calling the Indies.

bank.q: Leonardo da Vinci begins painting the Mona Lisa.
bank.w: Florence, about 1503 — he carried it with him for the rest of his life.

bank.q: Martin Luther posts his Ninety-five Theses.
bank.w: Wittenberg, October 1517 — the split that remade Europe began as a complaint about indulgences.

bank.q: William Shakespeare is born in Stratford-upon-Avon.
bank.w: April 1564 — his actual birthday is unknown; the record is his baptism.

bank.q: The Gunpowder Plot is foiled and Guy Fawkes is captured.
bank.w: November 5, 1605 — thirty-six barrels of gunpowder under Parliament.

bank.q: Newton publishes the Principia Mathematica.
bank.w: 1687, paid for out of Edmond Halley’s own pocket — the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

bank.q: Peter the Great founds St. Petersburg.
bank.w: May 1703 — a new capital raised from a swamp, by imperial decree.

bank.q: The Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence.
bank.w: Philadelphia, July 4, 1776 — news crossed the Atlantic by sailing ship, weeks later.

bank.q: Parisians storm the Bastille.
bank.w: July 14, 1789 — seven prisoners freed, one revolution begun.

bank.q: The United States concludes the Louisiana Purchase.
bank.w: 1803 — 828,000 square miles from Napoleon for about four cents an acre.

bank.q: Napoleon is defeated at Waterloo.
bank.w: June 18, 1815 — four days later he abdicated; the exile to Saint Helena followed.

bank.q: The Stockton & Darlington opens as the first public steam railway.
bank.w: September 1825 — Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first fare-paying passengers.

bank.q: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species.
bank.w: November 1859 — the first printing of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on day one.

bank.q: The American Civil War begins at Fort Sumter.
bank.w: April 1861 — the bombardment lasted a day and a half; the war lasted four years.

bank.q: The Suez Canal opens to shipping.
bank.w: November 1869 — it cut the London-to-Bombay run by thousands of miles.

bank.q: Alexander Graham Bell is granted the telephone patent.
bank.w: March 1876 — the same day he made the famous call to his assistant: "Mr. Watson, come here."

bank.q: The Eiffel Tower opens as the entrance arch to a world’s fair.
bank.w: March 1889 — critics called it a "useless and monstrous" tower. It was meant to come down in 1909.

bank.q: The first modern Olympic Games open in Athens.
bank.w: April 1896 — 14 nations, no women athletes, and a marathon winner who became a Greek national hero.

bank.q: The Wright brothers make the first powered airplane flight.
bank.w: December 17, 1903 — four flights at Kitty Hawk; the longest lasted 59 seconds.

bank.q: Ford introduces the Model T.
bank.w: October 1908 — "any color so long as it is black" came later; the price kept falling instead.

bank.q: The RMS Titanic sinks on her maiden voyage.
bank.w: April 15, 1912 — over 1,500 died in water just below freezing. The Californian never answered.

bank.q: The First World War begins.
bank.w: July–August 1914 — a Sarajevo assassination lit a fuse the whole alliance system had laid.

bank.q: The 19th Amendment is ratified, giving American women the vote.
bank.w: August 1920 — 72 years after Seneca Falls, decided by one state legislator’s mother’s advice.

bank.q: Howard Carter opens Tutankhamun’s tomb.
bank.w: November 1922 — "wonderful things" glimpsed through a small breach by candlelight.

bank.q: Lindbergh flies solo from New York to Paris.
bank.w: May 1927 — 33 and a half hours, dead reckoning, and a periscope because he couldn’t see past the fuel tank.

bank.q: Alexander Fleming discovers penicillin.
bank.w: September 1928 — a stack of forgotten petri dishes, one careless summer, one lucky mold.

bank.q: The Wall Street Crash wipes out the US stock market.
bank.w: October 1929 — Black Thursday, then Black Monday, then Black Tuesday, then a decade of it.

bank.q: The Hindenburg burns at Lakehurst, New Jersey.
bank.w: May 6, 1937 — "Oh, the humanity!" — 97 people aboard; 62 survived.

bank.q: The Second World War begins with the invasion of Poland.
bank.w: September 1, 1939 — the Luftwaffe hit Wieluń at 4:40 in the morning.

bank.q: D-Day: Allied forces land in Normandy.
bank.w: June 6, 1944 — the largest seaborne invasion in history, on five beaches and from the air.

bank.q: The first atomic bomb is tested at Trinity.
bank.w: July 16, 1945 — "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." Oppenheimer said he thought of it later.

bank.q: The Roswell incident makes UFOs a household word.
bank.w: July 1947 — a press release about a "flying disc," then a weather balloon, then fifty years of argument.

bank.q: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
bank.w: October 4, 1957 — a polished 58cm sphere that beeped at the whole world at once.

bank.q: President John F. Kennedy is assassinated in Dallas.
bank.w: November 22, 1963 — the Zapruder film exists because a dressmaker brought his camera to Dealey Plaza.

bank.q: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon.
bank.w: July 20, 1969 — Armstrong’s boot, a camera left behind to watch, and 600 million viewers.

bank.q: ARPANET sends its first message between two computers.
bank.w: October 29, 1969 — "LO." The intended "LOGIN" crashed the system after two letters.

bank.q: Saigon falls and the Vietnam War ends.
bank.w: April 30, 1975 — helicopters lifting off rooftops, the war’s most famous photograph taken from below.

bank.q: Apple Computer is founded in a garage in Cupertino.
bank.w: April 1, 1976 — three founders; the first product was a bare circuit board.

bank.q: The Chernobyl reactor explodes.
bank.w: April 26, 1986 — the announcement began with Swedish monitors noticing radiation that wasn’t theirs.

bank.q: The Berlin Wall falls.
bank.w: November 9, 1989 — a botched press conference and guards who stopped taking orders.

bank.q: The Hubble Space Telescope is launched.
bank.w: April 1990 — its first images were blurry; a 1993 servicing mission gave it glasses.

bank.q: Nelson Mandela is elected President of South Africa.
bank.w: May 1994 — a fully representative election, four years after leaving prison.

bank.q: The September 11 attacks
bank.w: September 11, 2001 — the morning the towers fell and the century found its shape.

bank.q: The iPhone goes on sale.
bank.w: June 29, 2007 — lines around Apple Stores; the App Store didn’t even exist until a year later.

bank.q: The Curiosity rover lands on Mars.
bank.w: August 6, 2012 — the seven minutes of terror, a sky-crane hover, and it stuck the landing.

bank.q: The last western Roman emperor is deposed, and the empire of the west ends.
bank.w: September 4, 476: the teenage Romulus Augustulus was packed off to a pension in Campania, the regalia went east to Zeno, and a barbarian officer ruled Italy.

bank.q: Charlemagne is crowned Emperor of the Romans in St. Peter’s, on Christmas Day.
bank.w: December 25, 800. Pope Leo III set the crown on his head during the Mass, and Byzantium spent centuries refusing to applaud.

bank.q: William of Normandy defeats Harold Godwinson at Hastings and takes the English crown.
bank.w: October 14, 1066. Harold died late in the day, and by Christmas a French-speaking duke was being crowned in Westminster.

bank.q: Ibn Battuta leaves Tangier on the first leg of a journey that will out-travel Marco Polo.
bank.w: June 1325, aged 21. By traditional count he covered some 75,000 miles across the Muslim world and beyond, several times Marco Polo’s route.

bank.q: The last ship of Magellan’s fleet completes the first circumnavigation of the globe.
bank.w: September 6, 1522: the Victoria limped into Seville with fewer than 20 of the original crew, and without Magellan, who had died in the Philippines.

bank.q: The Spanish Armada is defeated in the Channel and wrecked by storms on the way home.
bank.w: Summer 1588: 130 ships, unfavorable winds, fireships in the Calais roads, and North Sea storms that finished the job on the way home.

bank.q: The Great Fire of London destroys most of the old city in four days.
bank.w: September 2 to 6, 1666, starting in a bakery in Pudding Lane. It consumed 13,000 houses and 87 churches, and it broke the plague year’s back.

bank.q: The Louvre opens to the public as the republic’s national museum.
bank.w: August 10, 1793, with 537 paintings on the walls, most of them confiscated from the crown. A palace became public property in an afternoon.

bank.q: The Fourth Crusade, diverted from Jerusalem, storms and sacks Constantinople.
bank.w: April 1204: a crusade that never reached the Holy Land gutted Christendom’s greatest city instead, and the Venetians sailed home with its bronze horses.

bank.q: The Peasants’ Revolt reaches London and burns the Savoy Palace.
bank.w: June 1381: Wat Tyler’s army camped on Blackheath, burned the duke of Lancaster’s palace, and met the boy king face to face at Mile End.

bank.q: Gutenberg is first recorded with his movable-type press at Mainz.
bank.w: A lawsuit from 1439 had already let slip the secret press; by 1440 he was back at Mainz, and fifteen years later the Bible changed everything.

bank.q: Galileo observes the moons of Jupiter through his telescope.
bank.w: January 1610: four little stars that shuffled around Jupiter broke the Earth-centered sky for good. Naming them the Medicean stars was politics; the orbits were physics.

bank.q: Britain’s Slavery Abolition Act ends slavery in most of the British Empire.
bank.w: August 1833: Parliament voted freedom for the empire’s enslaved people, paying a vast fortune in compensation to former owners rather than to the freed.

bank.q: Revolutions sweep Europe from Paris to Vienna in the Year of Spring.
bank.w: Spring 1848: barricades rose in a dozen capitals and kings ran for the coast. By autumn nearly everywhere had been rolled back, but nothing was quite the same.

bank.q: The German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles, with Prussia’s king as emperor.
bank.w: January 18, 1871: proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors while Paris lay under siege, chosen as the spot so France would never forget.

bank.q: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat, and the Montgomery boycott begins.
bank.w: December 1, 1955: her arrest began a 381-day boycott that carried a 26-year-old pastor named Martin Luther King Jr. onto the national stage.

bank.q: Henry V’s outnumbered army wins the battle of Agincourt.
bank.w: October 25, 1415, St. Crispin’s Day: mud, arrows, and a French charge that bogged down ankle-deep. Shakespeare gave the king a better speech than the field did, but not by much.

bank.q: Ottoman forces under Mehmed II take Constantinople, ending the Roman Empire in the East.
bank.w: May 29, 1453: gunpowder finally beat the Theodosian Walls, Constantine XI died in the breach, and the city became Istanbul, capital of an empire that would rule from the Danube to the Nile.

bank.q: The Treaty of Paris ends the Revolutionary War and Britain recognizes the United States.
bank.w: September 3, 1783: signed in Paris almost two years after the guns stopped at Yorktown, it gave the United States everything to the Mississippi River and fishing rights off Newfoundland, which the new country would soon need more than it knew.

bank.q: French soldiers digging a fort near Rosetta unearth a stone carved three ways.
bank.w: July 1799: an officer of Napoleon’s expedition noticed a slab of black granite carrying hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek. Twenty-three years later Champollion read the top line, and Egypt’s sealed past opened.

bank.q: The Great Exhibition opens in Joseph Paxton’s Crystal Palace in Hyde Park.
bank.w: May 1, 1851: the world’s first world’s fair, a glass house built of mass-produced parts in months, drew six million visitors in half a year. The profits founded Kensington’s museum quarter, which was the point.

bank.q: A telegraph message crosses the Atlantic for the first time, from Queen Victoria to President Buchanan.
bank.w: August 16, 1858: the new cable under the Atlantic carried 99 words of congratulation in an hour, plus celebration fireworks and parades, and then died within weeks. The 1866 cable stuck, and stayed.

bank.q: Mahatma Gandhi is assassinated in Delhi.
bank.w: January 30, 1948: shot on his way to a prayer meeting by a Hindu nationalist, a martyr at 78. His ashes went to the rivers of India; his fasting had already stopped a civil war.

bank.q: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reach the summit of Everest.
bank.w: May 29, 1953: the ninth British expedition to the mountain was the one that stood on it. They spent about fifteen minutes on top, and left a hole in the snow for someone else to find.
